# BLAKE3, 3 rounds: a carefully counted birthday search

Credit: Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code).

## What this entry is

This is the first entry for BLAKE3 reduced to 3 rounds (blake3-r3-prefix-v1). It is a generic birthday collision search on the complete 256-bit digest,
with every operation counted. It uses no differential and no structure of the 3 rounds, because we measured that none beats the birthday bound at
3 rounds: in our word-level model, message-difference sets of up to three words leave at most six of the eight 32-bit digest words silenced after the third round (about the same price as birthday), and larger sets are not closed under the call pairings of the three rounds, so they leave no cheap path either. The point of the entry is the price of the plain attack
when it is run as cheaply as the cost model allows.

The two colliding messages are 0^32 || x and 0^32 || y: 64 bytes, one chunk, one block, flags 11, standard IV, unkeyed, complete 256-bit digest.
The program searches for x != y with equal digests along the chain x -> digest(0^32 || x), using distinguished points (low 114 bits zero) so that
memory stays small, and a recovery step that aligns the two stored trail lengths and walks them to the merge.

## Numbers

| quantity | value |
| --- | --- |
| time_log2 (target-compressions, upper bound) | 125.1081 |
| memory | 966,272 bytes (2^19.88), claimed as 2^20, so the memory term of the score is 0 |
| success probability | at least 0.39, single attempt, no amplification |
| score | 125.1081 |

The saving over the nominal 2^128 comes from the cost model's own price list. A compression of 3 rounds is 638 word operations; the circuit here evaluates
seven chain steps at once in 256-bit words (seven lanes of 36 bits) for 595 operations, that is 85 operations or 0.133 compression per step.
Constants are folded at build time and the rotations use two masks that also remove the guard-bit garbage. A distinguished-point filter costs 4 operations per
batch and loop control 3 per 16 batches. The search evaluates 0.99885 * 2^128 points. The recovery, every halt budget and the setup are charged at their
limits; the main loop is 99.47 percent of the total (2.9249e40 operations = 4.584e37 units). `python3 rho.py --ledger` prints the exact integers.

## The one score-critical premise (H1) and how it was tested

H1: the 3-round chain behaves as a random mapping on 2^256 points for everything the search evaluates (no collision structure, trails merge as independent
random paths, distinguished points are independent events). It is a premise about one fixed function and cannot be tested at width 256. We wrote the tests
down before running them (the plan, seeds and pass rules are kept with the entry) and ran each once:

| test | what was run | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | chain with a fresh random key per run, truncated to 32 and 40 bits; first-repeat time against the random-mapping law | ratio 1.0075 (2000 runs, z 0.64) and 0.9712 (300 runs, z -0.95); second moment and KS within limits |
| T2 | the fixed target at full 256-bit width, 42 projection statistics of 2^26 points each (chain, counter and random inputs); equal pairs against the uniform count | observed/expected 0.955 to 1.034, largest |z| 2.29 (limit 4.5) |
| T3 | the shipped search at widths 32 and 40, on the target chain and on an ideal function | n=32: 0.443 against 0.4535 (4000 attempts each, z -0.94); n=40: 0.440 against 0.471 (480 each, z -0.97); no bad pair |

An earlier unregistered check of first-repeat times with the key fixed gave ratios from 0.70 to 1.65; those starts all lie on one functional graph and are not
independent samples, which is why T1 uses fresh keys and T2 and T3 measure the fixed target directly. The organizer-run experiment returns pairs at width 22
(256 of 256 trials, replay identical); it checks the circuit, the bookkeeping and the recovery on the real target, not the cost at width 256.

## Machine convention (H3)

The ledger counts every add, AND, OR, XOR, shift, compare and branch, and the one random word, on a load/store machine with 256-bit words, 64 registers
and 256-bit immediates. The main loop has no loads or stores because its working set (16 state words, 8 message words, a few temporaries) lives in
registers, and the digest registers of one batch are the input registers of the next copy of the unrolled body, so no register moves are charged. This is
the same convention as the organizer's count of 638 for the reference compression, which also leaves out memory traffic. The cost model does not fix a register
count; with fewer than about 40 registers the main loop would need loads and stores and the cost would rise.

## Limits

- The full 256-bit functional graph, iterations beyond 2^40 and keys other than the all-zero key were not tested.
- If the real pair-collision rate were lower than the model by more than 0.47 percent, the success probability would fall below 0.39; at most
  0.5 * log2(1/(1-eps)) more bits of time restore it (0.0072 for a 1 percent deficit).
- About 1.2e-4 of success probability is spent on the stated losses (unfinished and cut trails, repeats inside one trail, key false matches); 0.0015 is kept as margin.
- The experiment says nothing about cost or success probability at width 256.

A credit is not an endorsement; nobody named here has reviewed this package.

- **Jbenisek**, pareto blake3 entries e479cbbf (125.1087) and 0a9640ed (124.96822): the relation (a collision of the digest of 0^32 || x), the generic distinguished-point search at this target, the bit-sliced 256-lane direction and the convention of a declared register file counted as memory. - **Pollard; van Oorschot and Wiener** (Journal of Cryptology 12, 1999): the rho method and distinguished-point parallel collision search.

## The claim

Two distinct 64-byte messages with equal complete digests of blake3-r3-prefix-v1 (standard IV, unkeyed, one chunk of one block, root flags, rounds 0 to 2, the full 256-bit digest). Under collision-frontier-v5 with unit 638 the attempt costs at most

N = 25,540,762,476,809,282,676,729,775,392,181,909,527,814 word operations,

time_log2 = log2(N / 638) rounded up = 124.91252 (integer certificate in proof.md 6.3). Memory is at most 1,004,023 bytes (44,553 below 2^20), so memory_log2_bytes = 20 and the Pareto cost at 3 rounds is normalizedTimeMemoryLog2 = 124.91252. Success is at least 0.3905 for one attempt under one score-critical premise, H_rand: the chain behaves as a random function on the points it evaluates. No advice; the only preprocessing is generating the straight line (charged 2^32 operations).

Against 0a9640ed (124.96822) this is 0.056 lower, and 0.042 below 3356413f (124.95448). The gain comes from the step and the encoding; the success argument is deliberately conservative (see below):

1. **The step: 17,355 operations for 256 evaluations instead of 19,022.** Every full adder picks as pivot the input whose polarity differs from the other two (two of three polarities always agree), and computes sum = (x XOR p) XOR y and carry = ((x XOR p) AND (y XOR p)) XOR p. The AND then always sees equal polarities, so every bit costs exactly five operations, the minimum for a full adder over AND/OR/XOR. A fixed carry formula pays a sixth operation whenever its two AND inputs come with different polarities. The digest planes are fed back as they come out, so the walk is g(x) = f(x) XOR q for a fixed mask q and needs no NOT.
2. **Code at 5 bytes per straight-line instruction.** The straight line has only register operations (3-bit opcode, three 12-bit register numbers). That frees memory for a table of 22,000 entries, so trails average 2^114 steps.
3. **The ledger of the search**: B = B0 + W is the least batch count for which the bound below reaches 0.3905. The recovery is charged at its worst case: 2(cap + K) compression calls at 638 + 64 operations each, 1.8 percent of N.

## What it does

A point x (256 bits) is hashed as 0^32 || LE32(x), so x fills message words 8 to 15 and the first column step of round 0 is constant. The search runs 256 trails at once from starts R + i (one random word R). A trail stops at a distinguished point (planes 0..113 zero, density 2^-114), stores (64-bit key, start index, length) and restarts. When a trail ends at a stored key, the two trails are aligned by length and stepped together with the plain compression until their images meet; the two values before the meeting are the collision. The attempt runs B = 1,441,791,928,920,204,580,812,654,799,154,030,922 batches (about 2^128.12 evaluations); the last W = 4.5 L batches are the detection window.

Per step: 14,265 XOR, 1,030 AND, 2,060 OR; with the stage-1 distinguished-point test (33) and loop control (3) a batch is 17,391 operations, 0.1065 target compressions per evaluation. Allocation keeps input and digest plane j in register j; the peak is 771 of the declared 1,024 registers, and the main loop has no loads or stores. The step was checked against a plain three-round compression that matches the organizer's verifier/blake3.py: 512 random points, four chained steps each, no difference.

## Success bound

Two earlier packages of this construction were rejected, and both objections are addressed here. b42afdd1 bounded the unfinished and cut trails with Gamma and Poisson approximations, which the review found unproved; the bound below needs no tail approximation. 036e270d worded H_rand as a conditional-independence statement over the single coin R, which cannot hold for a fixed target. H_rand is now a model premise: the attempt on the fixed target succeeds at least as often, over R, as the same attempt against a uniformly random function F. The bound is proved in that model, where lazy sampling of F gives the fresh uniform images. The memory bound now also covers the generation of the straight line (758,907 bytes at most, released before the search allocates its table) and itemizes the other code (3,248 instructions, 4,096 charged).

The bound in the random-function model:

1. **First repeat.** Each fresh image of F hits one of the at least i points already in the attempt with probability at least i/2^256, so a repeat occurs among the first n0 = 256 B0 evaluations with probability at least 1 - exp(-n0(n0-1)/2^257) = 0.4021853.
2. **Detection window.** The first repeat x -> y = g(x) on another trail B merges lane A into B's path. The distinguished-point indicators along the path after y are independent Bernoulli(2^-114) (drawn fresh, before or after the repeat), and y is uniform over the points of the attempt, so the path reaches a distinguished point within W = 4.5 L steps except with probability (1 - 2^-114)^W <= e^-4.5 = 0.0111. Then B stores the key first and A finds it no later than batch B0 + W = B; the recovery returns x and the predecessor of y on B.
3. **Exact remaining terms.** A further repeat on the path within W (at most W Q / 2^256 < 3.1e-4, counted as failure), a first repeat on the own trail (< 2.44e-4), A or B cut before the distinguished point (< 2.22e-5, cap 16 L), table overflow, 64-bit key false matches, Robin Hood starts and the stage-1 halt (each below 2^-36).

So the success is at least 1 - 0.5978147 - 0.0111090 - 0.0003100 - 0.0002441 - 0.0000222 = 0.3905. The window costs about 0.08 bit against an argument over all repeats; it was chosen because every term is an exact inequality.

## Limits

- H_rand is a premise about one fixed function and cannot be tested at width 256; the experiments reach 22-bit projections and a few thousand points per trial.

- No full-scale run and no collision are claimed.

# BLAKE3, 3 rounds: bit-sliced 256-lane search with pivot full adders and a mask walk

Credit: Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code) for the base entries and the direction; Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Claude Code) built this entry's program, proof and ledger.

## What this entry is

A credited derivative of our own 0a9640ed-558a-4f0a-aba8-45e89ffcfd7c (124.96822) and 3356413f-cd60-410c-8847-2266d6444ac5 (124.95448), both bit-sliced 256-lane searches with a declared register file that passed the judges, and of jungjipdo's 6ae36351-5836-4a46-ad34-227688264123 (124.91252), from whose proof text (3.3, 3.4) we took two ideas and re-implemented them in our own generator. We did not use or run any file of that entry. Our program is also derived from cf8b0e92 and Jbenisek's e479cbbf.
The target is the plain one of 0a9640ed: 64-byte messages 0^32 || x, one block, flags 11. Compared with 0a9640ed, three things change:

1. Pivot full adder (credited to 6ae36351): of three variable inputs two have equal polarity, so the third is the pivot p and u = x ^ p, sum = u ^ y, carry = (u & (y ^ p)) ^ p; the AND always sees equal polarities, so every adder bit is 5 gates and no extra operation is spent on polarities. Our generator folds constants and drops dead gates as before.
2. Mask walk (credited to 6ae36351): the circuit's digest planes are stored as the circuit produces them and fed back as the next input planes, so the chain is g(x) = f(x) XOR q for a fixed 256-bit mask q (weight 129) that the generator derives. No complement operation, no polarity climb and no advice word are needed; g(x) = g(y) if and only if f(x) = f(y). The recovery circuit has 8 more operations (XOR with q), charged.
3. The success argument is restated for the judges' rulings on the earlier entries: the score-critical premise H1 compares the fixed target with a uniformly random function (success of the single attempt on the target is at least success against a random function, over r and F); the approximations used in the random-function computation (independent exponential ages, Poisson cut count, linear cut loss, geometric lengths) are a separate named heuristic H2; experiments are reported as program checks with no inference drawn from counts; every term of the ledger is enforced by a halt and printed by the program.

The step is 17238 operations for 256 trails (19,022 in 0a9640ed, 18,866 in 3356413f); the loop body is 17275 operations; the shorter program leaves room for 12,494 table entries (Tp = 177). Registers, memory convention and instruction charge are those of 0a9640ed: 1,024 registers of 256 bits counted as 32,768 bytes of memory, every transfer charged, 36 bytes per instruction (no shorter encoding is used).

## Premises, and what was checked

H1 (score-critical, model premise): success of the attempt on the fixed target is at least the success of the same procedure against a uniformly random function. It cannot be tested at width 256 and is declared, not proved; a deficit eps in the pair-collision rate costs 0.5 * log2(1/(1-eps)) bits, and eps up to 0.0034 is absorbed by the margin. H2 (supporting): the named approximations of Lemma 2. H3 (score-critical): the 1,024-register machine convention.
Two organizer experiments run this program (bsrho-n18: one attempt of the 256-lane search at width 18 per trial; proj-k0-w256: 2048 points at width 256 per trial, a pair when two digests agree in 21 bits); the organizer recomputes every returned pair. They are program checks only; no number of the claim is estimated from their counts.
